headline: Brent jumps nearly 7% in a week to $117.38 as West Asia risks build, and India's oil basket averages about $120 in October
summary: Brent crude futures for December rose $7.52, or nearly 7%, last week to settle at $117.38 a barrel, while US WTI gained 4.3% to $103.27, as US-Iran tensions, Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz kept supply fears alive. Analysts quoted by PTI said any disruption to energy infrastructure or Hormuz shipping could push crude towards $120, while real progress towards de-escalation could bring a sharp fall; the US Federal Reserve's 27-28 October meeting is the other big trigger this week. Business Standard separately reported that the Indian crude basket has averaged around $120 a barrel so far in October, its highest since March 2012. EY India's D K Srivastava told BusinessLine that if crude stays about $20 above the RBI's $95 assumption, GDP growth for 2026-27 could slip to 7% from 7.1% and inflation rise to about 5.7% from 5.2%.
concept_note: Attacks on oil sites and threats to a key shipping lane raise the risk that less oil reaches the market, which shifts the supply curve to the left and pushes the price up. For India, which imports most of its crude, that higher price flows into fuel costs, inflation and the government's subsidy bill.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by BusinessLine
teaser_title: India now pays about $120 for a barrel of oil, the most since 2012. One shipping lane explains most of it.
teaser: Brent rose nearly 7% in a single week as traders priced in the risk to Saudi oil sites and the Strait of Hormuz. The worry is about how much oil can reach the market. The law of supply card shows what shifts the curve.

headline: Foreign investors pull ₹48,056 crore out of Indian shares in October, taking 2026 outflows to ₹3.08 lakh crore
summary: Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn ₹48,056 crore from Indian equities so far in October, after taking out ₹35,861 crore in September, according to depository data from CDSL. That takes their net outflow for 2026 to ₹3.08 lakh crore, far above the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025. Analysts blamed high crude prices, West Asia tensions, inflation worries and weak earnings, and said high US interest rates are making American assets more attractive. Selling eased in the week to 23 October, when FPIs were net buyers on two days as the US 10-year bond yield fell from 5.36% to about 5%. Separately, BusinessLine reported that the Nifty is down about 13% in the current Samvat year, on course to be the worst Samvat since 2014.
concept_note: A global investor's money can sit in Indian shares or in US bonds paying around 5%. When the safe US return rises and Indian prospects look riskier, the opportunity cost of staying in India goes up, and money leaves.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by The Hindu and BusinessLine
teaser_title: Foreign investors have pulled ₹3.08 lakh crore out of Indian shares this year, nearly double all of 2025.
teaser: October alone saw ₹48,056 crore leave, as US bonds near 5% and costly oil made India look less rewarding for the risk. Every rupee invested here is a rupee not earning elsewhere. The opportunity cost card explains the choice.

headline: Tata Motors' €3.91-billion bid for Iveco reaches its tender deadline with about 35% of shares tendered against the 80% it needs
summary: Monday, 26 October, is the scheduled last day for Iveco shareholders to tender their shares to Tata Motors, which needs 80% acceptance to complete its €3.91-billion takeover of the Italian truckmaker. Only about 35% had been tendered as of 22 October, BusinessLine reported, though managing director Girish Wagh told analysts that most shares are usually tendered in the final 24 to 48 hours. Tata raised its offer from €14.10 to €14.40 a share and called it final, but activist investor Petrus Advisers says Iveco is worth about €18; Petrus, Davidson Kempner and Syquant Capital together hold about 20.4%. Italy's industry minister wants commitments on jobs and plants, and unions want safeguards beyond two years. If it succeeds, the combined group would have about €21 billion in annual revenue and sell more than 590,000 vehicles a year, with settlement expected on 30 October.
concept_note: Shareholders want the highest price, while Italy's government and unions want jobs and factories protected. Tata has to satisfy owners and wider stakeholders at the same time, which is the tension the stakeholder view describes.
teaser_title: Tata Motors needs 80% of Iveco's shares by today. At last count it had about 35%.
teaser: Hedge funds want a higher price, Italy wants its factories kept and unions want jobs guaranteed, all while Tata calls €14.40 a share final. A takeover answers to more than shareholders. The profit vs stakeholder card shows why.

headline: India-US interim trade deal is stuck over tariffs, and New Delhi may wait until after the US mid-term elections, sources say
summary: The interim trade pact between India and the US remains stalled even though US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said it is 99% complete, BusinessLine reported, citing sources. Washington wants to keep the 18% tariff agreed in the February framework, but India says it cannot accept more than the 10% additional levy its exports currently face. The sources said the situation changed after the US Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs, making the older terms unattractive. India is also wary of agricultural concessions the US wants to show farm-state voters before the mid-term elections, and is inclined to wait until after the vote. New Delhi is further seeking assurances that any future US penalties would leave it with lower tariffs than rivals such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
concept_note: Tariffs, court rulings and elections abroad are political and legal forces that no single company controls, yet they decide what Indian exporters can charge in the US. These are the P and L of the PESTLE framework.
teaser_title: The US says the trade deal is 99% done. India says the last 1% is the tariff, and it won't budge.
teaser: Washington wants an 18% rate while Indian exports now face 10%, and New Delhi may wait out the US mid-term elections. An exporter's price in America depends on politics in two capitals. The PESTLE card explains these outside forces.

headline: Kolkata's Senco Gold to buy 68% of Melorra's parent August Jewellery for ₹68 crore to reach younger, online buyers
summary: Kolkata-based jeweller Senco Gold said on Sunday it has signed agreements to buy a 68% stake in August Jewellery Pvt Ltd, which runs the online jewellery brand Melorra, for ₹68 crore. The money will go in through fresh shares issued in several tranches, with completion targeted by February 2027, subject to conditions, the company said in a regulatory filing. Together with a stake bought by a promoter group entity, the holding will reach 79%, making August Jewellery a Senco subsidiary. Senco said the deal fits its digital and omnichannel strategy aimed at fast-growing young customers, and that Melorra's design and e-commerce skills should complement its own strengths. The funds will be used for growth and to clear existing liabilities, and no government or regulatory approval is needed.
concept_note: Young buyers often discover jewellery online, compare designs on their phones and then buy either on an app or in a store. By adding Melorra, Senco is trying to be present at every step of that looping, multi-channel decision journey.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by The Economic Times
teaser_title: A Kolkata jeweller is buying an online brand to win buyers who shop for gold on their phones.
teaser: Senco Gold will take 68% of Melorra's parent for ₹68 crore, betting on young customers who browse online and buy wherever is easiest. Today's shopper rarely moves in a straight line. The consumer decision process card explains the new journey.

headline: Godrej Properties expects record ₹41,500 crore of sales bookings this year, beating its ₹39,000 crore guidance
summary: Godrej Properties expects its sales bookings to rise about 22% this financial year to a record ₹41,500 crore, ahead of its guidance of ₹39,000 crore, chairperson Pirojsha Godrej told PTI. Bookings rose 7% to ₹16,659 crore in April to September, and he expects ₹22,500 crore to ₹25,000 crore in the second half, with October to December likely to be the company's best quarter ever thanks to launches in Mumbai's Bandra and Gurugram. Sales in already-running projects rose 83% to ₹5,054 crore in the September quarter. He said housing demand has held steady despite the uncertainty from the West Asia crisis. The company sold ₹34,171 crore of property last year.
concept_note: Guidance is a company's forecast of demand, built from launches planned, sales in running projects and market conditions. Godrej Properties is showing how a firm estimates the size of its market and then measures itself against that estimate.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by BusinessLine
teaser_title: Oil is near $120 and shares are falling, yet Godrej Properties expects a record ₹41,500 crore of home sales.
teaser: Bookings in its already-running projects jumped 83% last quarter, and it expects its best quarter ever from October to December. A sales target is really a forecast of demand. The market measurement card shows how firms make one.

headline: L'Oréal's global CEO says India is in a 'great turnaround', with double-digit growth and a push into quick commerce
summary: L'Oréal chief executive Nicolas Hieronimus said the group's India business is doing a 'great turnaround', helped by stronger teams, more products created for Indian consumers and faster online sales, especially through quick commerce. India posted double-digit growth in L'Oréal's consumer products division in the September quarter, according to the company's earnings update. Its region covering South Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Africa grew 19.2% on a like-for-like basis, with India and Indonesia accelerating on haircare and skincare. The company is taking its dermatological skincare brands CeraVe and La Roche-Posay to more Indian cities, with Hieronimus calling CeraVe 'still a baby brand' in India but growing fast.
concept_note: L'Oréal's turnaround came from creating more products for Indian needs and selling them where Indian buyers now shop, rather than pushing global products as they are. That is the shift from a product focus to a marketing orientation.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by The Economic Times
teaser_title: L'Oréal's CEO says India has turned around. The fix: products made for India, sold on quick-commerce apps.
teaser: India grew in double digits last quarter as L'Oréal tailored more products locally and leaned on quick-commerce apps. Starting from the customer rather than the product is an old marketing lesson. The marketing orientations card explains it.

headline: Government to pay up to half the cost of deepwater oil wells under ₹84,084-crore Samudra Manthan scheme, but wants repayment if they strike
summary: New operating guidelines for the ₹84,084-crore Samudra Manthan scheme say the government will fund up to 50% of the cost of 56 exploratory wells in deep and ultra-deep waters, capped at ₹675 crore a well, and up to 100% of four stratigraphic wells, capped at ₹1,350 crore each, Business Standard reported. If a well finds oil or gas, the operator must repay the support in yearly instalments, starting after seven years of commercial production or once it has recovered half its costs, whichever comes first, with no adjustment for inflation. If a well finds nothing, the state bears the loss. Only state-run firms or consortia they lead can apply, and only blocks awarded under the revenue-sharing regime since 2016 qualify. The scheme aims to cut India's reliance on imported oil and gas and runs to 2030-31.
concept_note: The government's right to be repaid exists only if a well strikes oil or gas, an uncertain future event. That is what accountants call a contingent asset: a possible gain that is not counted until it becomes virtually certain.
teaser_title: The government will pay up to ₹675 crore towards one deep-sea oil well, and gets repaid only if it strikes.
teaser: Under Samudra Manthan the state takes the loss on dry wells and claims a share back from the winners. A payment that depends on an uncertain event has a special name in accounting. The contingent assets card explains it.

headline: Emirates brings its Airbus A350 to the Kolkata-Dubai route and raises weekly flights to 12, citing rising demand
summary: Emirates has put its wide-body Airbus A350 on the Kolkata-Dubai route, and Millennium Post reported, citing the Airports Authority of India, that weekly flights between the two cities rise from 11 to 12. The aircraft arrived at Kolkata's Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose International Airport on Sunday and was given a water cannon salute. Airport director Vikram Singh pointed to growing demand for international travel as the reason for the expansion. Aviation schedule tracker AeroRoutes had earlier reported that Emirates planned to switch its daily Kolkata flight from a Boeing 777 to the A350 from 25 October. The extra service gives travellers from eastern India more options to connect through Dubai to Emirates' global network.
concept_note: When more people want to fly at the same fares, the whole demand curve shifts out, and the airline responds with a bigger plane and an extra flight. That is an increase in demand, not just a movement along the curve.
source_name: Millennium Post; also reported by AeroRoutes
teaser_title: Kolkata just got Emirates' A350 and a 12th weekly flight to Dubai. Travellers from the east are the reason.
teaser: The airport says demand for international travel from Kolkata is growing, so Emirates sent a bigger plane and an extra flight. When more people want something at the same price, the whole curve moves. The change in demand card explains the difference.

headline: China's stock market has lost $3.5 trillion since May as price wars and weak demand eat into company profits
summary: Chinese stocks have shed $3.5 trillion in value since a peak in May, and the CSI 300 index fell into a bear market last week, according to Bloomberg data reported by Business Standard. Investors are worried that a long consumer slowdown and fierce price competition are hurting earnings in sectors from banks to electric vehicles and AI. Battery maker CATL missed profit estimates, and MSCI China companies that have reported so far have missed forecasts by an average of 9%. Analysts said Beijing appears in no hurry to launch big new stimulus because the economy is slowing at a pace it can tolerate. Some cash-hungry internet giants have raised money by selling new shares, such as Alibaba's $10 billion share sale.
concept_note: When many rivals fight mainly on price, the intense rivalry among competitors drives profits down for everyone, even strong companies. China's price wars are Porter's 'rivalry among existing competitors' playing out across a whole stock market.
teaser_title: China's stock market has lost $3.5 trillion since May. Its own companies' price wars are a big reason.
teaser: Even battery giant CATL missed its profit estimate as rivals undercut each other, and Chinese firms are missing forecasts by an average of 9%. Too much rivalry can wipe out an industry's profits. Porter's five forces card shows how.

headline: Consumer regulator fines Hogar Technologies ₹1 lakh for walkie-talkie ads that left out licensing rules
summary: The Central Consumer Protection Authority has fined Kerala-based Hogar Technologies and Innovations ₹1 lakh for walkie-talkie advertisements and product listings that omitted key regulatory details such as operating frequencies and licence requirements, officials said on Sunday. The regulator said the omissions could lead buyers to believe the devices could be used legally without official authorisation; only personal radios in the 446.0-446.2 MHz band are exempt from licensing. In an earlier investigation, the CCPA found more than 16,970 non-compliant walkie-talkie listings and issued notices to 13 e-commerce firms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho and JioMart. It has passed final orders against 12 of them, with penalties totalling ₹58 lakh.
concept_note: An advert can mislead not only through false claims but by leaving out facts a buyer needs. Unlike harmless exaggeration (puffery), hiding that a product may need a licence can push a consumer into an illegal or wrong purchase.
teaser_title: An ad can mislead without saying anything false. A walkie-talkie seller paid ₹1 lakh for what it left out.
teaser: The regulator says leaving out frequency and licence details made buyers think the devices were legal to use, and it has already fined 12 shopping platforms ₹58 lakh in all. Where does selling talk end and misleading begin? The puffery card explains the line.

headline: GST tribunal says airlines can get back GST on cancelled tickets if they refunded both fare and tax to passengers
summary: The GST Appellate Tribunal has ruled that an airline can claim a refund of GST paid on cancelled tickets if it returned the full fare and tax to passengers and can prove it. The case involved eight refund claims totalling about ₹45.9 lakh by Singapore Airlines for October 2019 to March 2021, when Covid-19 forced it to cancel flights and refund passengers, but it could not adjust the credit notes against its output tax. Tax officials had rejected the claims; the tribunal's Ernakulam bench set that aside and ordered the refund to be processed within two weeks with interest. A tax expert told PTI that the ruling confirms GST should not become a cost when a sale is cancelled and the tax is fully returned.
concept_note: GST is meant to be a tax on the final consumer, with businesses passing it on and recovering what they pay through credits and adjustments. When a sale is cancelled and the customer gets the tax back, the business should not be stuck carrying it.
source_name: Business Standard (PTI); also reported by BusinessLine
teaser_title: Your cancelled flight was refunded, tax included. Should the airline still lose the GST? A tribunal says no.
teaser: Singapore Airlines returned fares and GST to passengers during Covid, then had to go to a tribunal to get about ₹45.9 lakh of tax back. GST is designed so businesses don't end up bearing it. The input tax credit card explains how.
